title: Did gladiators fight to the death?
hook: In films, nearly every fight ends with a body. In the real arena, the sums were different.
summary: Not always: gladiators were expensive and the loser could be spared; still, bones from a gladiator cemetery show that death in the arena was a real risk.
cardText: Not always. Gladiators were expensive, and the loser could be spared. Death was still a real risk, and the famous thumbs-down may never have existed.

cardBlocks.text: In the movies, two men walk into the arena and one walks out. But most gladiators were enslaved men who got hard training, a rich diet and expert medical care: an expensive investment. If one died, his owner could charge the sponsor up to a hundred times the price of a gladiator who survived. And it was the sponsor, listening to the crowd, who decided whether the loser was spared.

That didn’t make the arena bloodless. At Ephesus, in today’s Turkey, skeletons from a gladiators’ cemetery show wounds that had healed after earlier fights, and also fatal blows. Historians still argue about how often fights ended in death.
Killing a gladiator was costly and many losers were spared, but death in the arena was a real risk.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The details of the rules are lost, but mosaics show a referee, sometimes with an assistant, holding back the winner’s arm. Their presence suggests the rules were complex.

Graffiti scratched on walls record the debut of one Marcus Attilius. As a rookie he beat Hilarus, from the emperor Nero’s troupe, who had won 13 victory wreaths, and then Lucius Raecius Felix, who had 12. Both losers were spared.
What the bones of Ephesus say

The Ephesus cemetery, found in 1993 and dated to the second century AD, was studied by researchers in Austria who examined 67 gladiators. Ten had died from a hammer-like blow to the side of the head. The researchers think these were fighters the crowd had condemned who were still alive when carried out, and were finished off backstage.
The bones also revealed their diet: mostly vegetarian, heavy on grain. Writers of the time called gladiators “barley men”.

The Latin phrase pollice verso just means “with a turned thumb”; nobody knows which way it turned. The poet Martial says crowds asked for mercy by waving handkerchiefs or shouting. The thumbs-down idea took hold with Pollice Verso, a painting the Frenchman Jean-Léon Gérôme finished in 1872, which inspired the film Gladiator (2000).

Here the experts disagree. A historical film consultant says deaths were rare or accidental; the Ephesus researchers say their findings rule out the idea of a show in which hardly anyone died. A researcher at the University of California, Berkeley, notes that the death rate changed a lot over time.

claims.text: Most gladiators were enslaved men who received rigorous training, a high-energy diet and expert medical care, which made them an expensive investment.

support.excerpt: Most gladiators were slaves. They were subjected to a rigorous training, fed on a high-energy diet, and given expert medical attention. Hence they were an expensive investment, not to be despatched lightly.
Second, gladiators were expensive.

claims.text: For a gladiator killed in combat, the troupe’s owner could charge the sponsor up to a hundred times the price of one who survived.

support.excerpt: For a gladiator who died in combat the trainer (lanista) might charge the sponsor of the fatal spectacle up to a hundred times the cost of a gladiator who survived.

claims.text: The sponsor of the show, following the crowd’s wishes, decided whether a defeated gladiator was spared.

support.excerpt: It was the prerogative of the sponsor, acting upon the wishes of the spectators, to decide whether to reprieve the defeated gladiator or consign him to the victor to be polished off.

claims.text: Skeletons from the Ephesus gladiator cemetery show head wounds that had healed and also wounds suffered around the time of death.

support.excerpt: The best example is the gladiator cemetery at Ephesus, in which a minimum of 68 individuals were excavated. Eleven of these bodies showed evidence of well-healed antemortem cranial trauma, while ten had cranial injuries incurring around the time of death [3].
Many of the men Grossschmidt's team studied died only after surviving multiple blows to the head.

claims.text: Experts disagree on how often fights ended in death, and the death rate varied over time.

support.excerpt: Gladiator fights were only rarely, or accidentally, to the death.
the findings also dismiss any theory that gladiatorial combat was a kind of martial-arts show in which death was rare.
evidence indicates that the mortality rate of gladiators varied considerably over time.

claims.text: Nobody knows what the thumb gesture that decided a gladiator’s fate looked like; no historical record confirms thumbs-down as a death signal.

support.excerpt: Pollice verso translates simply as "turned thumb," but the manner or direction is not known.

While a modern read on this gesture suggests that a “thumbs down” was a signal that a defeated gladiator should be condemned to death (likely influenced by Ridley Scott’s feature film Gladiator), there are no historical records that confirm this.

his hand stayed (at least temporarily) by the umpire. The figure of the umpire is frequently depicted in the background of an engagement, sometimes accompanied by an assistant.
This suggests that gladiators were well matched in their capabilities, and followed sets of rules enforced by two referees.

claims.text: According to graffiti scratched on walls, the rookie Marcus Attilius beat Hilarus, of Nero’s troupe, holder of 13 wreaths, and then Lucius Raecius Felix; both losers were spared.

support.excerpt: As a mere rookie (tiro) he defeated an old hand, Hilarus, from the troupe owned by the emperor Nero, even though Hilarus had won the special distinction of a wreath no fewer than 13 times.
Both Hilarus and Raecius must have fought admirably against Attilius, since each of them was granted a reprieve (missio).
